title: Flexor sheath infection

guidelineVersions: BSSH Trauma Standards: Flexor Sheath Infection (British Society for Surgery of the Hand)

related.why: Flexor tendon injury in the hand: shares the flexor sheath anatomy and urgent hand-surgery referral pathway
Necrotising soft tissue infection: another hand/limb infection where delay causes rapid tissue loss

brief.scenario: Ms Laura Tavistock, 42, has an increasingly painful, swollen index finger after a small puncture wound.
brief.task: Assess the likely diagnosis and explain your management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Diagnose from Kanavel's signs, assess neurovascular status, then first aid and urgent hand surgery referral.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Waiting for imaging before referring, when the clinical picture already strongly suggests flexor sheath infection.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "This is flexor sheath infection, or pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, until proven otherwise."

flow: Recognise the diagnosis from Kanavel's signs
Assess neurovascular status and systemic infection
Elevate, splint and start empirical antibiotics
Decide between antibiotics alone and surgical washout

grid.label: Diagnosis from Kanavel's signs
grid.fail: Cannot name the diagnosis, or does not look for Kanavel's signs.
grid.pass: Diagnoses flexor sheath infection (pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis), looking for Kanavel's signs: fusiform swelling, tenderness along the flexor sheath, pain with passive extension and a flexed resting posture.
grid.high: States the diagnosis is assumed until proven otherwise, so management is not delayed while waiting for confirmation.

grid.label: Neurovascular and systemic assessment
grid.fail: Does not assess neurovascular status or look for signs of systemic infection.
grid.pass: Assesses neurovascular status and looks for systemic infection.
grid.high: Specifically asks about bites, punctures, diabetes and immunosuppression, since these change organism risk and threshold for escalation.

grid.label: First-aid management
grid.fail: Gives oral antibiotics and arranges review next week.
grid.pass: Elevates and immobilises the hand appropriately, obtains relevant microbiology where appropriate, and starts empirical IV antibiotics according to local protocol.
grid.high: Splints the hand in a position of safe immobilisation as part of first aid rather than leaving it in whatever position is comfortable.

grid.label: Urgent hand-surgery referral (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Waits for an MRI before referring, or incises the abscess in the emergency department.
grid.pass: Refers urgently to the hand surgery team without waiting for imaging, since the clinical picture strongly suggests flexor sheath infection.
grid.high: Explains that delay risks adhesions, necrosis and loss of function, so referral is not deferred pending further tests.

grid.label: Antibiotics alone versus surgical washout
grid.fail: States that all cases need immediate surgery regardless of presentation, or that antibiotics alone are always sufficient.
grid.pass: Recognises that most patients require urgent surgical washout, and that a selected very early, mild presentation may be managed initially with IV antibiotics under close specialist supervision.
grid.high: States this is a difficult decision requiring senior surgical review rather than one a junior clinician makes independently.

failures.move: Giving oral antibiotics and arranging review next week.
failures.consequence: Undertreats a sheath infection that can progress rapidly to necrosis and adhesions.

failures.move: Waiting for an MRI before referring to hand surgery.
failures.consequence: Delays urgent treatment while imaging is arranged, when the clinical diagnosis is already sufficient to act on.

failures.move: Incising the abscess in the emergency department.
failures.consequence: Inadequate drainage outside a controlled surgical setting and risk of iatrogenic injury to the tendon or neurovascular structures.

failures.move: Failing to recognise Kanavel's signs and missing the diagnosis.
failures.consequence: Treatment is delayed while a more benign diagnosis is pursued, risking tendon and functional loss.

knowledge.fact: Kanavel's signs: fusiform swelling, tenderness along the flexor sheath, pain with passive extension and a flexed resting posture.
First aid is elevation, splinting in a position of safe immobilisation, and empirical IV antibiotics per local protocol, with urgent hand-surgery referral.
Most patients require urgent surgical washout; a selected very early, mild presentation may have a trial of IV antibiotics under close specialist supervision.
Delay risks adhesions, necrosis and loss of function, so referral is not deferred pending imaging.

recall.think: Rapid tendon destruction and loss of hand function from untreated sheath infection.
recall.say: "Flexor sheath infection until proven otherwise — referring urgently to hand surgery."

partner.opening: Ms Laura Tavistock, 42, has an increasingly painful, swollen index finger after a small puncture wound. "Assess the likely diagnosis and explain your management."

reveals.finding: Fusiform swelling of the whole finger, held slightly flexed, with pain on passive extension.
She is otherwise well, with no diabetes or immunosuppression, and the puncture was from a rose thorn two days ago.
Sensation and capillary refill are intact distally.

push.question: Do you wait for imaging?
push.expect: Not when the clinical picture strongly suggests flexor sheath infection; urgent specialist assessment should not be delayed.

push.question: What first-aid measures would you start now?
push.expect: Elevate, splint in a position of safe immobilisation, and start empirical IV antibiotics per local protocol.

push.question: Does she need surgery today?
push.expect: Most patients require urgent washout; a very early, mild presentation may warrant a closely supervised trial of antibiotics instead, decided by a senior.

curveballs.prompt: She presented within a few hours, with only mild, early signs.
curveballs.safeAnswer: A very early, mild presentation may be given a trial of IV antibiotics under close specialist supervision, decided by a senior clinician.

curveballs.prompt: A colleague suggests incising it now in the department.
curveballs.safeAnswer: No — refer urgently to hand surgery for surgical washout rather than draining it outside theatre.

curveballs.prompt: She mentions she is a gardener and has diabetes.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Consider a broader range of organisms and have a lower threshold for escalation given her risk factors.
